label: The strategy contains a bet on someone else's behaviour
statement: Some part of this could fail even if the organisation executes everything it controls perfectly.
why_it_matters: This is the line between a plan and a strategy. If nothing depends on an outside party's response, there is no competitive claim to assess.
pass_signals: A claim about how customers or competitors will respond
An acknowledged way of losing that is not an execution failure
fail_signals: Every element is within unilateral control
Success defined as completing activities on time

label: The core claims could be wrong
statement: The central statements are specific enough that they would read as false if a competitor's name were substituted.
why_it_matters: Language every competitor would also endorse creates the feeling of alignment while leaving every real choice unmade.
pass_signals: Named customers, arenas, exclusions or magnitudes
A statement a rival would dispute
fail_signals: Customer-centric, innovative, world-class as load-bearing terms
Survives substitution of any competitor's name

label: Winning is defined so that it could be lost
statement: The definition of winning names a market condition that a competitor could deny them, rather than a financial result or an ambition.
why_it_matters: An aspiration nobody could contest gives no direction to any subsequent choice.
pass_signals: Winning stated in terms of a position with named customers
Possible to describe what losing looks like
fail_signals: Aspiration is a revenue, margin or share number
Aspiration is a vision any competitor would sign

label: Winning is defined for a named constituency
statement: The aspiration says in whose eyes the organisation intends to win - which customers, and which other groups whose judgement it cannot ignore.
why_it_matters: An aspiration with no constituency lets the arena be chosen for internal convenience, and leaves the organisation unable to say whose satisfaction would count as success.
pass_signals: A specific group of customers named
Other constituencies whose judgement matters identified, and the tension between them acknowledged
fail_signals: Winning defined only in the organisation's own terms
Constituency is 'the market', 'shareholders' or 'stakeholders' with no further specification

label: An arena is specified
statement: The strategy states which customers, offerings and channels it is competing in.
why_it_matters: Without an arena there is nothing for a way of winning to be true of.
pass_signals: Customers and offerings named
Scope stated on more than one dimension
fail_signals: Arena is the organisation's entire current footprint
Arena stated as a market size

label: The arena excludes something that hurts
statement: At least one exclusion is something the organisation could plausibly have pursued and someone internally wanted.
why_it_matters: Exclusion is what turns a description of the business into a choice, and it is the fastest available signal that a choice was made.
pass_signals: Named customers or segments left to others
An opportunity that would be declined if offered
fail_signals: No exclusions stated
Exclusions are markets the organisation could not serve anyway

label: All arena dimensions have been examined
statement: Offering, customer, geography, channel and stage of the chain have each been considered, including the ones that were inherited rather than chosen.
why_it_matters: Unexamined arena dimensions constrain the way of winning without anyone having decided that they should.
pass_signals: Channel and route to market addressed explicitly
Team can say which dimensions they chose and which they inherited
fail_signals: Channel absent from the strategy
Arena mirrors the current organisation chart

label: The arena can support attractive returns for someone
statement: Somebody in this arena earns returns worth having, so the problem is position rather than structure.
why_it_matters: 'We are not winning here' and 'nobody wins here' call for entirely different responses.
pass_signals: An existing player earns attractive returns
A structural reason returns are available
fail_signals: Every participant is losing money and the strategy is to try harder

label: Customers are defined by behaviour, not description
statement: The chosen customers are distinguished by what they are trying to accomplish and how they choose, not by size, sector or demographic band.
why_it_matters: A segment that shares no common decision offers nothing specific to win.
pass_signals: Description of what these customers are trying to get done
Behaviour that differs from excluded customers
fail_signals: Segments cut by revenue band, headcount or region only
Same offer aimed at every segment

label: There is insight, not just description
statement: The understanding of the customer would predict how they respond to something that does not exist yet.
why_it_matters: Research about existing offerings explains the past; insight into context is what allows a differentiated offer to be designed.
pass_signals: An account of behaviour in context that explains why they choose as they do
A surprising observation the team can defend
fail_signals: Only satisfaction scores and stated preferences
Customer understanding entirely secondhand

label: The desired action is named, at a scale and on terms that are sustainable
statement: A specific behaviour is stated for the people whose action the strategy needs, at a scale and on terms that would sustain the organisation. In a commercial setting the terms are price; where the action is not a purchase, they are whatever the person gives up - time, attention, effort, a donation, a change of practice - and whatever sustains the organisation providing it.
why_it_matters: Volume on unsustainable terms and good terms at insufficient volume are both failures, so both belong in the success condition. Stating the terms in the setting's own currency keeps the test honest for organisations that do not sell anything.
pass_signals: An observable behaviour named for a specific group
A sense of how many, and on what terms
Where there is no purchase, the cost to the person and the basis of sustainability are both stated
fail_signals: Success stated as awareness or engagement
Success stated as an internal milestone
Scale asserted with no account of what makes it sustainable
In a commercial setting, price left out entirely
context_note: Do not fail a social-sector, public, membership or internal-service strategy merely for the absence of a price. Assess the equivalent exchange instead, and see test:context_fit_acknowledged.

label: There is a promise to the customer
statement: The strategy states what is promised to the chosen customer, in terms the customer would recognise.
why_it_matters: The promise is what motivates the action; without it the strategy describes what the organisation will do rather than why anyone would respond.
pass_signals: A promise a customer could repeat in their own words
fail_signals: Only internal capability language
A promise that is a list of features

label: The promise is specific enough to be broken
statement: It would be evident, to the customer and internally, if the promise were not delivered.
why_it_matters: A promise nobody can fail is a promise nobody relies on, and it cannot be managed against.
pass_signals: Failure would be visible and attributable
Someone inside is accountable for it
fail_signals: Promise phrased so that it is always technically kept

label: User, chooser, payer and channel are distinguished
statement: Where different parties use, choose, pay for and distribute the offering, each has a stated desired action.
why_it_matters: A strategy that compels only the end user, while an intermediary controls the choice, will not produce the action it needs.
pass_signals: Separate promises where interests diverge
Intermediary's own upside stated
fail_signals: Single undifferentiated 'customer' where several parties are involved

label: There is a stated way of winning
statement: The strategy says why a customer in this arena would choose this organisation over the alternatives.
why_it_matters: Without this, the strategy describes where it will compete and what it will build, but never why it would win.
pass_signals: A reason for preference stated from the customer's side
fail_signals: How-to-Win box contains goals or activities
The reason is that the organisation will try hard

label: The way of winning is one logic, not a list
statement: The How-to-Win reads as a causal chain in which the elements need each other, rather than as items joined by 'and'.
why_it_matters: A portfolio of sensible improvements spreads investment evenly and produces no compounding advantage.
pass_signals: Because-therefore structure
Removing one element breaks the rest
fail_signals: Numbered list of programmes
Any item could be dropped without consequence

label: The logic resolves to lower cost or to difference customers pay for
statement: The way of winning lands on a structural cost position or on differentiation, and the trade-offs the other route would have required are acknowledged.
why_it_matters: An organisation that is neither can be attacked on price by the low-cost player and on value by the differentiated one.
pass_signals: One route chosen explicitly
Trade-offs of the unchosen route named
fail_signals: Best quality at the best price with no mechanism
Cost and premium programmes running in parallel

label: A cost claim rests on a different configuration of activities
statement: Where the route is cost, the advantage comes from doing different things or doing them differently, not from effort or temporary input prices.
why_it_matters: Cost positions that any competitor could match by trying harder are not advantages.
pass_signals: A named structural difference in the activity set
A competitor would have to give something up to match it
fail_signals: Cost advantage from discipline, scale assumed but unearned, or a supplier deal

label: Difference shows up in customer behaviour
statement: Where the route is differentiation, the difference changes what customers do - what they pay, whether they switch, whether they stay.
why_it_matters: Difference the customer does not value is cost carried without return.
pass_signals: Evidence of willingness to pay, switching or retention
Customers give something up to have it
fail_signals: Differentiators are internally admired features
Evidence is awards or internal opinion

label: The way of winning is not the arena's best practice
statement: The strategy asks the organisation to do something its strongest competitor would not choose to do.
why_it_matters: Adopting what the leaders already do cannot produce advantage over the leaders.
pass_signals: Something a named rival would decline
A choice that looks wrong from a competitor's position
fail_signals: Central logic is closing benchmark gaps
Nothing here would surprise a competitor

label: The arena and the way of winning need each other
statement: This way of winning works better in this arena than in the adjacent ones, and this arena is a poor fit for the obvious alternative ways of winning.
why_it_matters: Where-to-Play and How-to-Win are one paired choice; either alone can look reasonable while the pair is incoherent.
pass_signals: A reason the pairing is mutually reinforcing
The logic would weaken in a neighbouring arena
fail_signals: The way of winning would apply anywhere
The arena was chosen before any way of winning was considered

label: Every advantage claim names its comparison
statement: Claims of being better specify better than whom, at what, and in whose judgement - including what the customer does today instead.
why_it_matters: Improvement against one's own past is not evidence of advantage, and 'doing nothing' is often the strongest competitor.
pass_signals: Named alternatives including substitutes and the status quo
fail_signals: Comparisons only to the organisation's own history
Competitors appear only in a landscape slide

label: The strategy survives the competitor's response
statement: Named rivals' likely responses are stated, along with why those responses do not neutralise the strategy.
why_it_matters: Share comes from somebody, and that somebody gets to respond.
pass_signals: Specific rival, specific plausible response, specific reason it fails or is unattractive to them
fail_signals: No response anticipated
Rivals assumed to be slow or passive without reason

label: Copying would require giving something up
statement: A competitor who fully understood this strategy would have to sacrifice something they value to match it.
why_it_matters: Trade-offs, not secrecy, are what make advantage durable; anything a rival could simply add is copyable.
pass_signals: A named trade-off a rival would refuse
Advantage depends on a system rather than a single element
fail_signals: Barrier is a head start, a secret, or being first

label: There is an account of how the advantage is renewed
statement: The strategy says how the position gets re-earned - what the organisation will learn or invest in ahead of competitors - rather than assuming a barrier that holds.
why_it_matters: Advantage treated as permanent gets underfunded, and erodes before anyone is watching for it.
pass_signals: A statement of which questions this organisation works on ahead of rivals
An account of how the advantage could decay
fail_signals: Advantage described as a durable moat
Competitive picture frozen at today

label: The move is large enough to reach a different position
statement: This is a step towards a materially different position rather than a refinement of the current one, or the team can say why refinement is sufficient.
why_it_matters: Where the landscape has many peaks, incremental moves give encouraging feedback while leading to a local summit.
pass_signals: A stated target position that differs from today
Pilots tied to a specific choice they would unlock
fail_signals: Strategy consists of pilots and options
Success criteria are learning or engagement only

label: Each capability is traceable to the way of winning
statement: Every capability named would become less important if the How-to-Win changed, and the ones that would not are identified as table stakes.
why_it_matters: Capabilities that serve any strategy equally spread investment and produce distinction in nothing.
pass_signals: Each capability mapped to a step in the winning logic
Table stakes separated from distinctive
fail_signals: Capabilities named as 'digital', 'talent', 'data'
No capability would change if the strategy changed

label: The capabilities reinforce one another
statement: Some capabilities are valuable mainly because of the presence of the others.
why_it_matters: A reinforcing system is much harder to copy than any capability within it.
pass_signals: Named pairs that only work together
fail_signals: A flat list of independent competencies

label: Capability gaps are admitted and addressed
statement: Required capabilities the organisation does not have are named, with a route for each - build, buy, partner, or change the strategy.
why_it_matters: Assumed capability is the most common single point of failure inside an otherwise coherent strategy, and it surfaces late.
pass_signals: Honest gap list with owners and time
At least one gap the organisation has never demonstrated it can close, treated as a risk
fail_signals: Required capabilities stated as intentions
No gaps identified at all

label: Something changes in the management systems
statement: At least one measure, budget line, review, routine or incentive changes as a direct result of the strategy.
why_it_matters: Unsupported choices decay back to whatever the existing systems already reward.
pass_signals: A named change someone would notice within a month
fail_signals: Management systems box empty or filled with 'governance'
Same metrics and meeting agendas as last year

label: Non-financial indicators track the critical conditions
statement: The conditions the logic depends on have observable indicators attached, which would move before the financials.
why_it_matters: Otherwise the organisation learns its theory was wrong from the income statement, after the cheap correction window has closed.
pass_signals: Indicators derived from the must-be-trues
Something measurable within the current quarter
fail_signals: All measures are financial or share
First checkpoint is a year out

label: Each choice has a named owner and boundaries
statement: It is clear who makes each choice and what they may decide without escalation.
why_it_matters: Unowned choices get made by default, inconsistently, by whoever is nearest the problem.
pass_signals: Named owners with stated decision rights
fail_signals: Ownership at committee level only
Nobody can say who decides

label: Money and attention move to match the choices
statement: Something is being defunded or deprioritised to fund the strategy, not only added.
why_it_matters: Where resources actually go is the organisation's operative strategy, whatever the document says.
pass_signals: A named reduction or exit
Senior time reallocated
fail_signals: All new initiatives, no reductions
Funded from unspecified efficiencies

label: Genuinely different possibilities were on the table
statement: At least one alternative differed in Where-to-Play, was specified well enough to evaluate, and was set aside for a stated reason.
why_it_matters: The quality of a decision is bounded by the quality of the alternatives considered.
pass_signals: A second possibility with a different arena
A reason it was rejected that refers to what would have had to be true
fail_signals: Alternatives named only to be dismissed
All options share the same arena

label: The must-be-true conditions are written down
statement: The conditions that would each have to hold for this to be a great choice are stated as falsifiable claims about the world.
why_it_matters: Until the logic is reverse-engineered, nobody can tell which part of the theory is load-bearing.
pass_signals: Conditions spanning customers, competitors, capabilities, channel and economics
Each written so it could be shown false
fail_signals: No assumptions stated
A risk register with mitigations instead of conditions
Conditions phrased as intentions

label: The least believed condition is identified
statement: The team can say which must-be-true they believe least, and why.
why_it_matters: The decision turns on the doubtful condition; effort spent confirming what everyone already believes is wasted.
pass_signals: A named barrier
Disagreement located on a specific condition
fail_signals: All conditions asserted with equal confidence
The most sceptical person's doubt is unrecorded

label: The barriers have cheap, decisive tests
statement: For each barrier there is a test that could change the team's mind, with pass and fail criteria agreed in advance.
why_it_matters: Tests designed after the data arrives always pass; tests aimed at undoubted conditions teach nothing.
pass_signals: Cheapest sufficient evidence identified
Pass and fail thresholds set beforehand
fail_signals: Testing plan is more analysis of the whole opportunity
No result would change the decision
No date by which the choice is made

label: There is a date by which the choice gets made
statement: The team has said when it will decide, and what it would choose if no further evidence arrived.
why_it_matters: Delay is a choice in favour of the status quo, usually made without anyone owning it.
pass_signals: A decision date
A stated default choice absent new evidence
fail_signals: Next step is always another piece of work
Nobody can say what evidence would be sufficient

label: Confidence is proportionate to the evidence
statement: The strategy does not present judgement as calculation, and its quantification is used where data can actually settle a question.
why_it_matters: Manufactured certainty makes a choice harder to revisit later, because it looks proven rather than chosen.
pass_signals: Stated where the team is betting rather than knowing
fail_signals: Multi-year projections to the decimal
Analysis whose every possible result supports the same recommendation

label: No step depends on what others ought to do
statement: Every assumption about another party's behaviour is justified by that party's own interests.
why_it_matters: A bet on other people's virtue is not a competitive asset.
pass_signals: Each external party's upside stated in their terms
fail_signals: 'Customers should value', 'the market will recognise'
Partner cooperation or competitor restraint assumed without reason

label: What would prove this wrong is agreed in advance
statement: The team has named the observations, and a timeframe, that would mean the strategy should change.
why_it_matters: Without this, every disappointing result is absorbed as an execution problem and the strategy becomes unfalsifiable.
pass_signals: Specific observable signals with a review point
fail_signals: Nothing would count as evidence against
Shortfalls consistently explained as delivery issues

label: Somebody gave something up
statement: The choices cost the organisation something it wanted - an opportunity declined, a capability deprioritised, a constituency's priority traded away.
why_it_matters: A strategy in which nobody lost anything has usually not been decided, only assembled.
pass_signals: A named trade-off and who bore it
fail_signals: Every constituency's priority survived
Multiple stated top priorities

label: The choices reinforce each other in both directions
statement: Reading the cascade down, each choice makes the next easier; reading it up, each choice is necessary to the one above.
why_it_matters: Strategies fail as often from individually sensible choices that do not add up as from obviously bad ones.
pass_signals: Both passes complete without a break
Tensions between choices named and resolved
fail_signals: Boxes filled independently
A capability or system that serves no stated choice

label: The strategy can be stated without the document
statement: The user can state the choices in a few plain sentences that name the customer, the arena, the way of winning and what is excluded.
why_it_matters: A strategy the people making daily choices cannot state cannot guide those choices.
pass_signals: A short spoken version that survives without slides
fail_signals: Requires the deck
People a level or two down describe something different

label: Functions and units have something to choose differently
statement: At least one function or unit can say what it now chooses differently, and what it will stop doing, because of this strategy.
why_it_matters: A function whose plans would be identical under a different corporate strategy has made no strategic choice.
pass_signals: A function's own arena and way of winning, in service of the whole
fail_signals: Corporate strategy restated at function level
No function has changed anything

label: Borrowed frameworks are inputs, not the strategy
statement: Where a tool or framework is present, the team can say which question it answered and which cascade choices remain open.
why_it_matters: A completed template supplies a strong feeling of rigour, which conceals missing choices more effectively than an empty page would.
pass_signals: The tool is described as feeding a choice rather than being one
The team can name what the tool does not settle
fail_signals: Objectives and key results, a scorecard or a canvas presented as the strategy
The artefact is organised around a template rather than around choices

label: The setting is established before the standards are applied
statement: The kind of organisation and arena is clear - commercial, social sector, regulated, monopoly, startup - and what would count as winning has been stated in terms that fit it.
why_it_matters: Tests written for a branded commercial business mark sound strategies in other settings as deficient for reasons that do not apply, which destroys the credibility of the whole assessment.
pass_signals: The setting is stated and the definition of winning suits it
Where there is no purchase or no direct rival, the desired action and the alternatives are still named
fail_signals: Commercial framing applied to an organisation that has no customers in that sense
The team cannot say what winning would mean in their own setting

label: The choices made downstream are governed by the strategy
statement: The team can name choices made below the leadership level that the strategy should shape, and say what the people making them have to go on.
why_it_matters: Most of what is later called execution is choice-making at a distance from the centre. A strategy that never reaches those choices cannot be said to have been implemented.
pass_signals: Specific recurring downstream choices named, with the guidance available for them
An example of a downstream choice that changed because of the strategy
fail_signals: Shortfalls consistently attributed to execution or discipline
Nobody can name a downstream choice the strategy governs

label: The centre earns its place
statement: Where several businesses are owned together, there is a stated reason each is better off inside this parent than as a competently owned standalone.
why_it_matters: Without it, corporate strategy reduces to a funding mechanism, and a weak business strategy is relocated rather than fixed.
pass_signals: A named contribution from the centre that a standalone owner could not supply
The businesses share something that would be costly to replicate separately
fail_signals: The centre's role is capital allocation and reporting only
Diversification offered as the answer to a weak position

label: The method aims at being right, not merely repeatable
statement: The team can say why their process would surface a right answer, not only a consistent one, and where its consistency might be hiding an error.
why_it_matters: A reliable process applied to a strategic question produces defensible wrong conclusions, and its very consistency makes them hard to challenge.
pass_signals: Acknowledgement of where the process could be consistently wrong
Qualitative evidence admitted alongside what is countable
fail_signals: Confidence rests on the process having been followed
Only what is measurable was allowed into the decision

label: The possibilities were generated, not just gathered
statement: At least one possibility on the table did not exist before this work started, rather than all of them being variants of current operations.
why_it_matters: Teams evaluate options competently and generate them badly; if every option is an extrapolation of today, the choice set is the real constraint.
pass_signals: A possibility that had to be invented, with an account of where it came from
Options that differ in arena, not only in degree
fail_signals: Every option is a variant of the current operating model
Options were assembled from what is already being proposed internally
